body.en: Sequences, series, and complex number arithmetic comprise approximately 10% of the EST II Math Level 1 exam. Candidates are evaluated on deriving explicit and recursive terms for arithmetic and geometric progressions, evaluating finite partial sums using Gauss and geometric formulas, determining the convergence of infinite geometric series, and manipulating complex numbers ($i = \sqrt{-1}$) in rectangular form.

label.en: Definition 3.1 — Progressions, Sigma Notation, and the Complex Field

body.en:
Core mathematical definitions and structural formulas:
  • Arithmetic Sequence (AP): A sequence with constant difference \(d = a_{n} - a_{n-1}\):
    \[ a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)d \]
    The arithmetic mean between two terms \(a\) and \(b\) is \(M = \frac{a + b}{2}\).
  • Geometric Sequence (GP): A sequence with constant common ratio \(r = \frac{a_n}{a_{n-1}}\) (\(r \neq 0\)):
    \[ a_n = a_1 \cdot r^{n-1} \]
    The geometric mean between positive terms \(a\) and \(b\) is \(G = \sqrt{ab}\).
  • Sigma Notation (\(\sum\)): The compact summation of terms from index \(k = m\) to \(n\):
    \[ \sum_{k=m}^n a_k = a_m + a_{m+1} + \dots + a_n \]
    The number of terms in the summation is \(N = n - m + 1\).
  • Complex Number Modulus and Conjugate: For \(z = a + bi\) with \(a, b \in \mathbb{R}\):
    1. Complex Conjugate: \(\bar{z} = a - bi\).
    2. Modulus: \(|z| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\), representing the Euclidean distance from the origin in the complex plane.
    3. Conjugate Product: \(z \bar{z} = |z|^2 = a^2 + b^2 \in \mathbb{R}\).

label.en: ● Deep Conceptual Intuition — Sequences, Series & Complex Numbers

body.en: Algebraic & Geometric Duality of \(\mathbb{C}\): Every complex number \(z = x + iy\) corresponds bijectively to a point \((x, y)\) in the Argand plane with modulus \(r = |z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) and principal argument \(\theta = \arg(z) \in (-\pi, \pi]\). In exponential Euler form, \(z = re^{i\theta} = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)\), multiplication scales moduli and adds arguments: \(z_1 z_2 = r_1 r_2 e^{i(\theta_1 + \theta_2)}\).

label.en: Theorem 3.1 — Series Summation Formulas and Infinite Convergence

body.en:
Analytical formulas for finite series and convergence criteria:
  • Arithmetic Series Summation (Gauss Formula):
    \[ S_n = \frac{n}{2}(a_1 + a_n) = \frac{n}{2}\left[2a_1 + (n - 1)d\right] \]
  • Finite Geometric Series Summation: For \(r \neq 1\):
    \[ S_n = \frac{a_1(1 - r^n)}{1 - r} = \frac{a_1 - r a_n}{1 - r} \]
  • Infinite Geometric Series Convergence Criterion: An infinite geometric series converges to a finite sum if and only if \(|r| < 1\):
    \[ S_\infty = \lim_{n \to \infty} S_n = \frac{a_1}{1 - r} \quad (|r| < 1) \]
    If \(|r| \ge 1\), the series diverges and no finite sum exists.
  • Powers of the Imaginary Unit \(i\): Powers of \(i\) cycle with period 4:
    \[ i^{4k} = 1, \quad i^{4k+1} = i, \quad i^{4k+2} = -1, \quad i^{4k+3} = -i \quad (k \in \mathbb{Z}) \]

caption.en: Convergence interval \(|r| < 1\) for an infinite geometric series. The sum to infinity \(S_\infty = \frac{a_1}{1 - r}\) converges strictly inside \((-1, 1)\) with open endpoints; the series diverges for \(|r| \ge 1\).

label.en: ▲ EST II Math Traps & Pitfalls — Sequences, Series & Complex Numbers

body.en:
• Infinite Geometric Series Convergence: The sum formula \(S_\infty = \frac{a_1}{1 - r}\) is valid only when \(|r| < 1\). If \(|r| \ge 1\), the series diverges and has no finite sum. If a question asks for the sum of \(3 - 6 + 12 - 24 + \cdots\), the answer is "diverges", not \(\frac{3}{1 - (-2)} = 1\).
  • Powers of \(i\) Modulo 4: The imaginary unit follows a 4-term repeating cycle: \(i^1 = i\), \(i^2 = -1\), \(i^3 = -i\), and \(i^4 = 1\). To evaluate \(i^n\), divide \(n\) by 4 and take the remainder \(r\): \(i^n = i^r\) (where remainder 0 corresponds to \(i^0 = 1\)). For negative powers: \(i^{-1} = -i\).
  • Complex Division & Conjugate: Never divide terms individually. To evaluate \(\frac{a + bi}{c + di}\), multiply numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate \(c - di\). The denominator becomes the real number \(c^2 + d^2\).
  • Sigma Indexing Traps: Watch the lower limit of summation! \(\sum_{k=1}^n c = nc\), but \(\sum_{k=0}^n c = (n+1)c\). In general, the number of terms is \(\text{upper} - \text{lower} + 1\).

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Sequences, Series & Complex Numbers)

body.en:
Why De Moivre's Theorem & Conjugate Root Pairing Hold: By Euler's identity \(e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\), raising \(z = re^{i\theta}\) to the \(n\)-th power gives:

\[ z^n = \left(re^{i\theta}\right)^n = r^n e^{in\theta} = r^n(\cos(n\theta) + i\sin(n\theta)) \]

Furthermore, if \(P(z) = \sum_{k=0}^n a_k z^k\) has real coefficients (\(a_k \in \mathbb{R}\)), taking complex conjugates across \(P(z_0) = 0\) uses \(\overline{z_1 + z_2} = \bar{z}_1 + \bar{z}_2\) and \(\bar{a}_k = a_k\) to prove \(P(\bar{z}_0) = \overline{P(z_0)} = 0\). Thus non-real roots of real polynomials always occur in conjugate pairs \(\alpha \pm i\beta\).

label.en: Worked Example 3.A — Arithmetic Progression Term & Sum Determination

body.en:
The 4th term of an arithmetic sequence is 17 and the 10th term is 41.
(a) Find the first term \(a_1\) and common difference \(d\).
(b) Calculate the sum of the first 25 terms \(S_{25}\).

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. (a) Set up a linear system for \(a_1\) and \(d\):
    \[ a_4 = a_1 + 3d = 17 \]
    \[ a_{10} = a_1 + 9d = 41 \]
    Subtract the first equation from the second:
    \[ (a_1 + 9d) - (a_1 + 3d) = 41 - 17 \implies 6d = 24 \implies \mathbf{d = 4} \]
    Substitute \(d = 4\) to find \(a_1\):
    \[ a_1 + 3(4) = 17 \implies a_1 + 12 = 17 \implies \mathbf{a_1 = 5} \]
  2. (b) Compute \(S_{25}\):
    Find the 25th term:
    \[ a_{25} = a_1 + 24d = 5 + 24(4) = 5 + 96 = 101 \]
    Apply the arithmetic series sum formula:
    \[ S_{25} = \frac{25}{2}(a_1 + a_{25}) = \frac{25}{2}(5 + 101) = \frac{25}{2}(106) = 25 \times 53 = \mathbf{1325} \]

label.en: Worked Example 3.B — Infinite Geometric Series & Repeating Decimals

body.en:
Express the repeating decimal \(0.\overline{27} = 0.272727\dots\) as an exact fraction in lowest terms using an infinite geometric series.

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. Decompose into an infinite geometric series:
    \[ 0.\overline{27} = \frac{27}{100} + \frac{27}{10000} + \frac{27}{1000000} + \dots \]
  2. Identify initial term \(a_1\) and common ratio \(r\):
    \[ a_1 = \frac{27}{100}, \qquad r = \frac{1}{100} \]
  3. Verify convergence:
    Since \(|r| = \left|\frac{1}{100}\right| = 0.01 < 1\), the infinite series converges.
  4. Calculate the sum \(S_\infty\):
    \[ S_\infty = \frac{a_1}{1 - r} = \frac{\frac{27}{100}}{1 - \frac{1}{100}} = \frac{\frac{27}{100}}{\frac{99}{100}} = \frac{27}{99} = \mathbf{\frac{3}{11}} \]
The exact fraction is \(\mathbf{\frac{3}{11}}\).

label.en: Worked Example 3.C — Complex Number Quotients & Modulus Calculation

body.en:
Given the complex number \(z = \dfrac{3 + 5i}{1 - 2i} - 2i^{17}\):
(a) Write \(z\) in standard form \(a + bi\).
(b) Compute the exact modulus \(|z|\).

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. (a) Simplify the fraction using conjugate multiplication:
    \[ \frac{3 + 5i}{1 - 2i} = \frac{(3 + 5i)(1 + 2i)}{(1 - 2i)(1 + 2i)} = \frac{3 + 6i + 5i + 10i^2}{1 - 4i^2} = \frac{3 + 11i - 10}{1 + 4} = \frac{-7 + 11i}{5} = -\frac{7}{5} + \frac{11}{5}i \]
  2. Simplify \(2i^{17}\):
    \(17 = 4(4) + 1 \implies i^{17} = i^1 = i\). Thus \(2i^{17} = 2i\).
  3. Combine the terms:
    \[ z = \left(-\frac{7}{5} + \frac{11}{5}i\right) - 2i = -\frac{7}{5} + \left(\frac{11}{5} - \frac{10}{5}\right)i = \mathbf{-\frac{7}{5} + \frac{1}{5}i} \]
  4. (b) Compute modulus \(|z|\):
    \[ |z| = \sqrt{\left(-\frac{7}{5}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{5}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\frac{49 + 1}{25}} = \sqrt{\frac{50}{25}} = \sqrt{2} \approx \mathbf{1.414} \]

label.en: Worked Example \(D\) — Sequences, Series & Complex Numbers (Easy Application)

body.en:
Problem (Easy): A sequence is defined by the recursive relation \( a_{n+1} = 2a_n \) with the first term \( a_1 = 5 \). What is the third term of this sequence?

Step-by-Step Solution: The sequence is defined by \( a_1 = 5 \) and \( a_{n+1} = 2a_n \). We need to find the third term, \( a_3 \). First, find the second term, \( a_2 \), using the recursive relation with \( n=1 \): \( a_2 = 2a_1 \) \( a_2 = 2(5) \) \( a_2 = 10 \) Next, find the third term, \( a_3 \), using the recursive relation with \( n=2 \): \( a_3 = 2a_2 \) \( a_3 = 2(10) \) \( a_3 = 20 \) Therefore, the third term of the sequence is 20.

label.en: ▲ Exam Pacing & Verification Strategy — Sequences, Series & Complex Numbers

body.en: Exam Verification Tip (Egyptian Scholastic Test (EST II — Math Level 1)): Always check complex division \(\dfrac{z_1}{z_2}\) by verifying that \(|z_1 / z_2| = |z_1| / |z_2|\). If the moduli ratio does not match, you multiplied the denominator by \(a + bi\) instead of the conjugate \(a - bi\).

question.en: Let \(z = \dfrac{5 + 2i}{2 - 3i} + i^{43}\). (a) Express \(z\) in standard form \(a + bi\). (b) Compute the modulus \(|z|\).

solution.en:
(a) Simplify the quotient and power of \(i\):

  • First evaluate \(\dfrac{5+2i}{2-3i}\): multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate \(2+3i\): \[ \dfrac{(5+2i)(2+3i)}{(2-3i)(2+3i)} = \dfrac{10 + 15i + 4i + 6i^2}{4 - 9i^2} = \dfrac{10 - 6 + 19i}{4 + 9} = \dfrac{4 + 19i}{13}. \]
  • Now evaluate \(i^{43}\): \(43 = 4(10) + 3\), remainder 3, so \(i^{43} = i^3 = -i = -\dfrac{13i}{13}\).
  • Combine terms: \[ z = \dfrac{4 + 19i}{13} - i = \dfrac{4 + 19i - 13i}{13} = \dfrac{4 + 6i}{13} = \mathbf{\dfrac{4}{13} + \dfrac{6}{13}i}. \]

(b) Modulus \(|z|\): \[ |z| = \sqrt{\left(\frac{4}{13}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{6}{13}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\frac{16 + 36}{169}} = \sqrt{\frac{52}{169}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{52}}{13} = \mathbf{\dfrac{2\sqrt{13}}{13}} \approx 0.555. \]

Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \(i\).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

question.en: An infinite geometric series has first term \(a_1 = 18\) and sum to infinity \(S_\infty = 24\). (a) Find the common ratio \(r\). (b) Calculate the third term \(a_3\).

solution.en:
(a) Find common ratio \(r\): \[ S_\infty = \frac{a_1}{1 - r} \implies 24 = \frac{18}{1 - r} \implies 1 - r = \frac{18}{24} = \frac{3}{4} \implies r = 1 - \frac{3}{4} = \mathbf{\frac{1}{4}}. \]

(b) Calculate 3rd term \(a_3\): \[ a_3 = a_1 \cdot r^2 = 18 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2 = 18 \cdot \frac{1}{16} = \mathbf{\frac{9}{8} = 1.125}. \]

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Sequences, Series & Complex Numbers and start from \(a_1 = 18\).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \(r\).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

solution.en:
Step 1: Identify geometric series parameters: For \(k = 1\), \(a_1 = 3(2)^0 = 3\). The common ratio is \(r = 2\) and the number of terms is \(n = 6\).

Step 2: Apply finite geometric sum formula: \[ S_6 = \frac{a_1(1 - r^6)}{1 - r} = \frac{3(1 - 2^6)}{1 - 2} = \frac{3(1 - 64)}{-1} = \frac{3(-63)}{-1} = 3 \times 63 = \mathbf{189}. \]
